records.current_summary: Turkey presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration. The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades.

prison_adds.title: Rights groups urge probe into 'suspicious' death of transgender prisoner in Turkey (Stockholm Center for Freedom)
prison_adds.summary: SCF (18 Dec 2025): transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and Turkish rights groups (coordinated from Human Rights Association / IHD branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakir, Mersin and Aydin) demanded an independent investigation and changes to 'detention practices affecting transgender prisoners'. Kaos GL-cited accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers say four transgender inmates were collectively sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators only entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; opposition MP Sevda Karaca (EMEP) raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025. The case documents that Turkey holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex (a trans man was held in a women's prison) and that trans-prisoner custody conditions were formally contested at the state level in late 2025.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQI+ prisoners are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches (Kaos GL), reporting the Prison Insider 'Country Profile' on Turkey (with CİSST data)
prison_adds.summary: Kaos GL (7 May 2024), covering the Prison Insider Country Profile report on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using ILGA World data: LGBTI+ prisoners in Turkish prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. CISST observations quoted in the article state that there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that Turkish prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. The piece documents that Turkey manages trans and LGBTI+ prisoners through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.

records.current_summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming.

prison_adds.title: Uruguay to build prison for transgender inmates — MercoPress
prison_adds.summary: MercoPress (29 Jul 2023), citing Uruguayan authorities and officials: as part of a new prison planned for Montevideo there will be a specific sector for the trans population, which Parliamentary Commissioner for the prison system Juan Miguel Petit called 'good news for a very vulnerable population' and estimated would be ready in less than two years. National Rehabilitation Institute (INR) Director Luis Mendoza told a parliamentary hearing that 'if the trans person enters the system they have the right to decide if they want to go to a men's or women's prison,' and that while trans women are currently placed in female prisons, cohabitation entails 'a whole process' of adaptation; he also noted the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for the trans population, adding 'the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line.' The article cites official figures of 14,965 people deprived of liberty, including 28 trans women and nine trans men (Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System).

records.current_summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — an unusual case: a tiny 0.49 km² tourist enclave with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile — the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists — but this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism: the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

prison_adds.title: Crime in Vatican City
prison_adds.summary: Vatican City operates no prison system: the article states there are only a few cells used for pre-trial detention, and persons sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serve their time in Italian prisons, with costs covered by Vatican City. Because no domestic prison system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case for this jurisdiction. (Last-resort encyclopedic source; no separate State Department Holy See chapter for 2023/2024 exists.)

records.current_summary:
Vietnam is broadly workable — described as one of the most tolerant countries in the region toward sexual minorities. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the 2015 Civil Code (Article 37) was a landmark recognising transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the implementing Gender Affirmation Law has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented here. Conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma and "red tape" in accessing care, and trans-competent providers are scarce.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, unrestricted bathroom access, and no criminalisation — but the stalled recognition means no practical gender-marker change on documents. This country is under one-party authoritarian rule, where an international human-rights organisation finds that "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice"; a UN development agency is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies.

prison_adds.title: Social News 16/1 — Separate jails proposed for transgender, gay prisoners
prison_adds.summary: VietnamNet (16 Jan 2015) reports a proposal by the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute to Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security to house homosexual and transgender prisoners in jails separate from the general prison population, to protect them from sexual harassment; the institute cited US California statistics that 67% of homosexual and transgender prisoners had suffered sexual harassment and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. Critically for the placement lane, the institute stated that under Vietnam's then-current prison infrastructure transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population — i.e. no housing wing matched to the prisoner's gender identity existed — and asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome or newer documented placement practice was found in the two search rounds conducted.
